transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Honestly, the main thing that finally made me book the appointment is this issue I keep having at work, especially in these long sales strategy meetings. I’m in advertising sales, so there are a lot of meetings where I’m supposed to just sit there, listen, take things in, maybe contribute at the right moment—but I keep finding myself getting up.

Like, I know I’m supposed to stay seated. It’s not that I don’t understand the expectation, and I’m not trying to be rude or disruptive. But after a while I’ll suddenly be up refilling my water, or walking over toward the printer, or kind of pacing for a minute like I’m checking on something, even if there isn’t really a good reason. It’s embarrassing because I can feel people noticing, and then I’m thinking, “Why did I just stand up again?” but in the moment it feels almost automatic, like sitting still through the whole thing is weirdly hard.
When you get up in those meetings, does it happen because a sudden wave of panic hits you?

No, I don’t think it’s panic, exactly. I mean, I know what you mean—like a sudden rush of fear or feeling like something terrible is happening—and that’s not really what it feels like.

It’s more like I just get this uncomfortable urge to move, or I’ll realize I’ve already stood up before I’ve fully thought it through. I might feel embarrassed afterward, or tense because I know it probably looks odd in a meeting, but I wouldn’t describe the thing that makes me get up as panic. It’s not like my heart suddenly drops and I need to escape or anything like that. It’s more… I don’t know, restlessness, I guess, but not in a dramatic way.
Do these times when you feel unusually restless happen in distinct episodes that are different from your usual self?

I’m not totally sure I’d call them distinct episodes, no. It doesn’t feel like, “Oh, here’s this separate state I go into for a while and then I come back to normal,” if that makes sense.

It feels more woven into how I am day to day, just more obvious in certain situations—like when I’m stuck sitting still and expected to be quiet and focused for a long time. I’m not noticing some big shift where I feel like a completely different version of myself. It’s more like the same restlessness gets turned up depending on the setting.
Do you often have trouble staying focused on tasks or conversations, even when you want to pay attention?

Yes, I do. That’s actually one of the things I notice a lot, especially at work. Like in longer strategy meetings, I’ll really intend to listen—I’m not sitting there thinking, “I don’t care,” or anything. I’ll start out following the discussion, looking at the slides, trying to track the point someone is making, and then a few minutes later I realize I’ve been staring at the same slide and I have no idea what the last point was.

It happens with client briefs too. I’ll open one up and genuinely want to read it carefully because it matters for my job, but I’ll get through a paragraph and then realize I didn’t absorb it at all. Sometimes my eyes are still moving across the words, but my brain is just… not holding onto it. Then I have to go back and reread the same section, sometimes more than once, which is frustrating because it’s not like the material is impossible or I don’t understand it. It’s more that my attention just kind of slips away without me noticing right away.

And in conversations, especially if they’re longer or there are a lot of details, I can miss pieces even though I’m trying to stay engaged. Then I feel awkward because I don’t want to ask someone to repeat something they literally just said.
Did you have these kinds of attention or restlessness problems when you were a child?

Yes, definitely. I mean, I didn’t think of it as a “problem” at the time, because I was a kid and I guess I thought that was just how I was, but looking back it was there really early—like elementary school, way before high school.

I remember teachers writing things like I was bright, but I rushed through my work or talked out of turn. And homework was a whole thing—I’d forget to bring it home, or I’d do it and then forget to turn it in, or it would be crumpled somewhere in my backpack. My desk was always stuffed with half-finished papers and random worksheets, like this messy pile of things I meant to finish or had started and then abandoned.

So yes, it wasn’t something that just showed up as an adult. It’s just that now the consequences are more obvious.
